skill.name: linux-production-shell-scripts
skill.description: Provides Bash script templates for Linux administration, including backups, monitoring, log analysis, network checks, cron scheduling, and service management.
skill.summary: Reusable Linux administration shell script templates for controlled production workflows.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: Most static command-execution hits are Markdown code fences, inline examples, or expected Bash syntax inside a shell-scripting template. I confirmed risks where examples intentionally use sudo, modify crontab, inspect local accounts or network state, call hardcoded external hosts, delete files, or execute remote scripts.

remediation.suggestion: Add explicit review, dry-run options, and operator confirmation before sudo, user management, package installation, or service control examples.
Require user authorization before reading account lists, hostnames, kernel details, network interfaces, or password expiry metadata.
Make scheduled tasks opt-in, idempotent, named, logged, and paired with clear removal instructions.
Add path allowlists, dry-run output, deletion previews, and safeguards against root or broad directory targets.
Require explicit host allowlists, script review, and least-privilege SSH accounts before generating remote execution commands.
Replace public default hosts and URLs with user-provided endpoints or documented placeholders.

The package installation template runs apt-get through sudo and can alter the host package set. Privileged installation needs explicit operator approval.
The service template restarts a system service through sudo. This can disrupt production availability if used on the wrong service or host.
The service template starts a system service through sudo. Privileged service control changes host state and should require confirmation.
The limitations section states that many templates require root or sudo privileges. That accurately signals elevated-impact scripts that need strong execution controls.
The uptime checker curls hardcoded public websites. This is legitimate monitoring syntax but can disclose connectivity tests to external services.
The network check template pings hardcoded public resolvers and google.com. This creates outbound traffic to third parties and should be parameterized for the user environment.
The .git check is standard repository detection before running git commands. It does not read hidden secrets or traverse unrelated hidden files.
The /proc/loadavg read is a standard health-check metric in a system report template. It does not access secrets or modify host state.

The password expiry checker intentionally reads /etc/passwd to enumerate users with bash shells. Even without password hashes, this exposes account inventory and supports local reconnaissance.
The crontab command appears in a quick-reference table rather than in an executable script block. The actual scheduling template is assessed separately as persistence risk.
The user creation template queries whether a local account exists before changing it. This is low-impact system reconnaissance tied to an administrative action.
The system information template writes a report filename containing the hostname and date. This can expose host identity in generated artifacts.
The system information collector records the hostname. Hostname collection is expected for inventory but still reveals local system identity.
The system information collector records uname output. Kernel and operating system details can support fingerprinting if shared outside the host.
This line is generic usage guidance and does not collect host, user, process, or network data. It is not evidence of system reconnaissance.
The network interface script records interface addresses and routing data. This is legitimate troubleshooting but reveals local network topology.
The combination appears because the skill teaches normal shell scripting and scheduling workflows. I found no obfuscation, evasion, hidden payload, or stealth installation in the skill file.

semantic_findings.title: Scheduled Task Persistence Template
semantic_findings.description: The cron setup example appends a task to the user crontab, which can create persistent recurring execution on a host.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The referenced lines define a schedule and pipe a new entry into crontab. This is a clear persistence mechanism even though the stated use is automation.

semantic_findings.title: Destructive File Deletion Template
semantic_findings.description: The cleanup example deletes files older than a user-supplied age under a user-supplied directory, which can remove important data if misconfigured.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The template accepts directory and age parameters and uses find with rm. The behavior is explicit destructive deletion, so confidence is high.

semantic_findings.title: Remote Script Execution Template
semantic_findings.description: The remote execution example sends a local script to a remote server over SSH and runs it with bash, enabling arbitrary remote command execution if misused.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The lines define remote_server and remote_script variables, then execute the script through ssh. The purpose is direct remote execution.

content.value_statement: Linux teams need repeatable scripts for backup, monitoring, cleanup, and service tasks. This skill provides reusable Bash templates that Claude, Codex, or Claude Code can adapt for controlled systems.
actual_capabilities: Provides Bash templates for directory, remote, database, and rotating backups.
Shows CPU, disk, system health, and log monitoring patterns.
Includes templates for user creation and password expiry reporting.
Covers network connectivity, website uptime, and interface inspection scripts.
Includes cron scheduling, package installation, service restart, cleanup, and git update examples.
Documents common Bash patterns for arguments, dates, permissions, and background execution.
limitations: Templates require review before use on production systems.
Several examples assume Linux, Bash, and common GNU utilities are available.
Some scripts need elevated permissions and can change system state.
Network and system inventory examples may expose host details if run without controls.

use_cases.title: Create Server Maintenance Scripts
use_cases.description: Draft backup, cleanup, and monitoring scripts for authorized Linux servers.

use_cases.title: Standardize DevOps Automation
use_cases.description: Prepare cron, package setup, service restart, and git update workflows for reviewed environments.

use_cases.title: Collect Operational Evidence
use_cases.description: Generate system health, log review, and network inspection scripts for approved incident workflows.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Backup Script
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a Bash backup script for this directory and destination. Include clear variables, logging, and a safe retention setting.

prompt_templates.title: Add Monitoring Alerts
prompt_templates.prompt: Create CPU and disk monitoring scripts for a Linux server. Include thresholds, log output, and comments for adding notifications.

prompt_templates.title: Harden a Cleanup Script
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this cleanup workflow and generate a safer Bash script with dry-run mode, path validation, and explicit confirmation.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Production Runbook
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a production shell automation plan for backups, monitoring, cron scheduling, and rollback. Include assumptions and operator checks.

output_examples.input: Create a daily backup workflow with seven-day retention.
output: A Bash backup template with configurable source and destination paths.
A retention section that removes older backup archives after validation.
A short checklist for testing restore behavior before production use.

output_examples.input: Prepare a disk and CPU health report for one server.
output: A monitoring script outline that records timestamps, load, memory, disk use, and top processes.
Suggested alert thresholds and log file naming conventions.
Notes about required permissions and local utility dependencies.

output_examples.input: Plan a safe service restart automation.
output: A restart workflow with status checks before and after the action.
Rollback and troubleshooting notes for failed starts.

best_practices: Test every generated script in a non-production environment first.
Use dry-run mode, explicit paths, and operator confirmation for destructive actions.
Review all sudo, cron, network, and account-management commands before execution.
anti_patterns: Do not run generated scripts as root without reviewing every command.
Do not hardcode production credentials, hosts, or secrets in templates.
Do not schedule background jobs without ownership, logging, and removal instructions.

faq.question: Does this skill execute shell commands automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides shell script templates and patterns. Users must review and run any generated script themselves.

faq.question: Can I use the templates on production servers?
faq.answer: Yes, but only after testing, code review, and approval from the system owner.

faq.question: Which systems are supported?
faq.answer: The examples target Linux or Unix systems with Bash and common tools such as rsync, openssl, curl, and systemctl.

faq.question: Do any examples require elevated permissions?
faq.answer: Yes. Package installation, service control, user management, and some account reports may require sudo or root privileges.

faq.question: Can the scripts be customized?
faq.answer: Yes. Paths, thresholds, hosts, schedules, packages, and log locations should be adapted to the target environment.

faq.question: What should I review before running a generated script?
faq.answer: Review file deletion, network calls, cron changes, sudo commands, account access, and any path that targets production data.
